title: Noach: the window (Genesis 6:16)
hookLine: the ark had a tzohar for light; midrash says it was a glowing stone

lines: THE DOOR IS SHUT, MONTH AFTER MONTH.
cards: Forget the picture-book ark with a giraffe's head poking out the top. The Torah's ark is a huge wooden box, sealed with pitch inside and out, three decks, crowded with animals and Noah's family.
The rain falls for forty days. The door is shut; the text says God shut it. Then the waiting, month after month as the text counts them, inside.
How does anyone live in a closed box that long? The blueprint God gives Noah is only a few verses. But one line in it is about light.

teach.h: TZOHAR: A RARE WORD FOR LIGHT.
teach.b: God tells Noah to make a tzohar for the ark, and finish it a cubit from the top. What's a tzohar? It's a rare word, and nobody is completely sure.
Some readers hear in it tzohorayim, noon, the brightest part of the day, so something to do with light. The rabbis in the midrash offer two answers, and Rashi repeats both.
One teacher says it was a window, an opening near the roof. Another says it was a precious stone, a gem that glowed and lit the ark from within. A window lets light in from outside.

teach.h: A WINDOW, OR A GLOWING STONE.
teach.b: A glowing stone makes light inside, even when outside is dark. The window says: even in a flood, keep one opening to the world; don't seal yourself in completely.
The stone says: when there's no light outside at all, carry some within. Much later, Hasidic teachers played with a different word in the same verse.

teach.h: TEIVAH: AN ARK, AND A WORD.
teach.b: The Hebrew for ark, teivah, also means a word. So when God tells Noah to come into the teivah, they heard: come into the word.

Step inside the words of your prayer, or your study, and make them a shelter with a light in them. And some readers notice what the plan leaves out: no rudder, no oars, no sail. Noah, as the text tells it, doesn't steer.
What he could do was make sure there was light inside.

how: Jewish readers study the tzohar with Rashi and the midrash, and Hasidic teachers use the double meaning of teivah, ark and word, to teach about entering the words of prayer.

o: the ark's door, which God himself shut
the pitch that sealed the ark against water
a source of light: a window, or a glowing stone

games.q: inside the ark — tap the pairs.
p: an ark, and also a word

s: the meaning of tzohar is certain
it's a rare word; the rabbis themselves give two answers.
Rashi gives two answers: a window or a precious stone
he repeats both from the midrash, without choosing.
the ark had a rudder so Noah could steer
the Torah describes no rudder, oar or sail.

games.q: you're Noah. the door has been shut, the rain is falling, and it's dark inside the ark. what did God tell you to build for this?
o: a rudder to steer out of the storm.
games.why: a tzohar. the rabbis say a window, or a glowing stone. either way: light inside when you can't steer.

practice: Think of something that feels like a flood right now, a worry, a hard stretch.

Find one window, one person or place that opens onto the world outside it, and then one stone, a small light you carry inside: a memory, a word, a reason. Rest your attention on that light, and let it glow.

wordCard.voice: Tzohar. The ark's source of light, a rare word: a window, some say, and some say a glowing stone.

orig.note: Hebrew: a source of light for the ark; some connect it to tzohorayim, noon.

carryVoice: Your line: make a window. A window or a stone, and either way, light. That's one hundred sixty-seven days.
